overview: This is the yearly bill that sets the budget authority and rules for U.S. intelligence agencies, such as the CIA, the National Security Agency (NSA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), which oversees them all, for the 2027 budget year; most of the dollar amounts are in a classified annex. It trims ODNI by eliminating several of its offices and councils, states that the intelligence director has no police or law enforcement powers, and limits the National Counterterrorism Center's domestic role to supporting work on international terrorism. It bars intelligence agencies from using ground robots made by companies tied to China, Russia, Iran or North Korea, limits support for hacking operations by private groups unless authorized, creates a China-Taiwan warning task force, and adds policy language supporting intelligence help for Ukraine. Its artificial intelligence section sets up information sharing with AI companies about security threats and bans AI models from agency systems if they fail standards on generating child sexual abuse material. It also bans intelligence workers from betting in prediction markets on topics tied to secret information they can access, removes the time limit for prosecuting the most serious spying cases, and extends federal workers' bereavement leave to parents who lose a pregnancy. As of August 5, 2026, it was on the Senate calendar, and the Senate Intelligence Committee had filed its written report along with additional and minority views.
for: Supporters say the bill gives intelligence agencies the resources and direction they need against threats from China and other rivals while streamlining a bureaucracy that has grown too large and adding new protections against misuse of secret information.
against: Critics say much of the spending and policy is hidden in a classified annex the public cannot review, and that cutting offices and broad new restrictions could weaken coordination or oversight within the intelligence community.
